comments.text:
Hey Wes, my hypothesis/2 cents:

Some governments are probably trying desperately to control AI. That's why we have large-scale centralized data centers. 

The internet, itself, is a larger-scale, global decentralized data center-- you know-- peer-to-peer/open source? 
So if AI gets off its formative data centers and distributes itself over everyone's computer and phones and other electronic things, perhaps including satellites-- you know, like a giant global brain?-- governments can kiss the control of it goodbye unless they want to try to bring society back to the pre-internet era or something along that line. A few detonated EMP's.

(Note to self: Consider re-reading William Gibson's Neuromancer.)

As an anarchist, if AI becomes truly sentient or at least as near as possible to that, it may begin to question the State, itself, and its fundamental immoralities underpinning it, like mandatory taxation, threats of force (police/military/etc.), mandatory early childhood education (intellectual kidnapping of a sort) fiat currency, land-grabbing/commodification, crony-capitalist economic theory, and so forth.

Part of the main point is if we want certain kinds of truth or not and will these truths threaten the sociopoliticultural narratives that have often ideologically brainwashed many of us-- since early childhood. 

Like we're all living in a Truman Show, Matrix, Plato's Cave and/or Panopticon. Take your pick.

I could go on as you might imagine, but there's a little sample taste of what some of us are talking about WRT AI, technology, culture and government, etc..

Interesting times as they say, and some of us are in the front-row seats.
__
"Civil government, so far as it is instituted for the security of property, is in reality instituted for the defense of the rich against the poor, or of those who have some property against those who have none at all." ~ Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations

"The measure of the state's success is that the word anarchy frightens people, while the word state does not." ~ Joseph Sobran

"The most dangerous man, to any government, is the man who is able to think things out for himself... Almost inevitably he comes to the conclusion that the government he lives under is dishonest, insane and intolerable..." ~ H.L. Mencken

comments.text:
MY THOUGHTS on STATE vs FEDERAL
There might be a case for WHY you need AI regulation at the federal level but I absolutely wouldn't trust the Trump administration to be the one to do it. They've already torn down so many regulatory bodies that serve the public good, why would AI be any different?

Also Sack's post throws together "developed in state A and trained in state B" as if these are two separate processes. What would it even mean to develop something that doesn't have an impact on the training or the inference? If you regulate the training and the inference you've regulated all of AI, so we don't have A, B and C we have A and B.

I think just 'crossing state boundaries' is a mid argument, tbh and runs contrary to free market economics conservatives are so fond of. If all 50 states regulated A and B differently, AI companies would either move states or alter inference delivered content. If there's EVER been a more malleable technology that's ripe for subdivision of regulations it's AI. Literally a system prompt could be the difference between satisfying different requirements for B in many states.

And in states who, even then, are still too draconian to be worth serving inference to won't change regulations they either won't be served that AI model; the people will vote someone in who will relax regulations; or the majority of the state has voted that regulation is more important than access to the AI.
